item.title: AI could help unlock more oil — and emissions
item.description:
Move over, data centers. AI's climate impact may extend well beyond the electricity it consumes.

Why it matters: A new peer-reviewed study finds AI could help produce more oil and natural gas — and produce a climate impact the authors argue could far outweigh the technology's benefits for renewable energy.

Driving the news: The research, just published in a Nature journal, concludes AI's role in boosting oil and gas production would outweigh its climate benefits from accelerating renewable energy, leading to a net increase in emissions under a range of scenarios.

  • The study is among the first to estimate how AI-driven gains in fossil fuel production could affect global emissions.

"Most assessments of AI's climate impact are framed as a tradeoff between data center energy use and the emissions AI might help avoid through renewables and efficiency gains," said Holly Alpine, co-author of the paper.

  • "What's missing from that calculation entirely is the other side of the same ledger: the emissions enabled from using AI to make fossil fuel production cheaper and more profitable," Alpine said.

Holly Alpine and Will Alpine, former Microsoft employees who founded the nonprofit initiative Enabled Emissions Campaign in 2024, co-led the study with researchers from Purdue University and an independent researcher.

How it works: AI can help oil companies find new resources and recover more from existing fields. It can also help renewable energy by improving forecasting and operations. The new study argues the fossil-fuel gains are likely to dominate.

By the numbers: The researchers estimate AI could add emissions equal to roughly 1% to 5% of the global energy sector's 2024 emissions under the scenarios they modeled.

  • The study estimates those emissions would be roughly three to 13 times the International Energy Agency's estimate of current data-center emissions.

The other side: A spokesperson for the American Petroleum Institute, the oil industry's main trade group, disputed the idea that more energy and lower emissions are in conflict.

  • "The U.S. oil and natural gas industry is continuing to produce more energy while reducing emissions by investing in better technology, implementing stronger operational practices and supporting science-based policy," API spokesperson Andrea Woods said in a statement.

State of play: The oil industry's embrace of AI has accelerated over the past two years.

  • Producers like Chevron, ExxonMobil, ADNOC and Aramco say AI is helping identify promising drilling prospects and improve recovery from existing fields.
  • Oilfield-service giants SLB, Halliburton and Baker Hughes are deploying AI to guide drilling and optimize well placement.
  • Analysts and consultancies, from Goldman Sachs to Wood Mackenzie, argue AI could lower production costs and increase economically recoverable reserves.

The big picture: AI is a general-purpose technology that can boost productivity in both fossil fuels and clean energy. Some experts argue the more important question is which applications society chooses to prioritize.

What they're saying: "I think cleantech is going to win anyway, so let's just focus on how we unlock clean energy resources with AI," said Brian Janous, who previously worked with Holly Alpine at Microsoft and now runs data center developer Cloverleaf Infrastructure.

  • "I'm glad Will and Holly are doing what they're doing. I'm not sure what it's going to change, but at least it puts pressure on," he said.

Zoom in: The researchers used a computer model of the global economy that estimates how AI-driven productivity gains ripple through energy markets.

  • Across the study's 64 modeled scenarios, emissions declined only when fossil-fuel productivity gains from AI were zero, Holly Alpine said.
  • The finding suggests that supporting renewable energy alone "will not get us" to lower emissions.

Yes, but: The model doesn't attempt to estimate AI's potential to accelerate cleantech breakthroughs such as fusion or long-duration storage.

  • "There is a lot of AI dreaming out there," said Michael Lazarus, senior scientist emeritus at the climate research group Stockholm Environment Institute who advised the authors on the study. "I don't know how one would anticipate that and model it."

What we're watching: The study's authors are making a call that echoes that of many others working at the intersection of AI and environmental issues: more transparency.

  • "If we can start with transparency about the effects, then we can start to think about how to govern it," said Will Alpine.
item.content:encoded:
Move over, data centers. AI's climate impact may extend well beyond the electricity it consumes.

Why it matters: A new peer-reviewed study finds AI could help produce more oil and natural gas — and produce a climate impact the authors argue could far outweigh the technology's benefits for renewable energy.

Driving the news: The research, just published in a Nature journal, concludes AI's role in boosting oil and gas production would outweigh its climate benefits from accelerating renewable energy, leading to a net increase in emissions under a range of scenarios.

  • The study is among the first to estimate how AI-driven gains in fossil fuel production could affect global emissions.

"Most assessments of AI's climate impact are framed as a tradeoff between data center energy use and the emissions AI might help avoid through renewables and efficiency gains," said Holly Alpine, co-author of the paper.

  • "What's missing from that calculation entirely is the other side of the same ledger: the emissions enabled from using AI to make fossil fuel production cheaper and more profitable," Alpine said.

Holly Alpine and Will Alpine, former Microsoft employees who founded the nonprofit initiative Enabled Emissions Campaign in 2024, co-led the study with researchers from Purdue University and an independent researcher.

How it works: AI can help oil companies find new resources and recover more from existing fields. It can also help renewable energy by improving forecasting and operations. The new study argues the fossil-fuel gains are likely to dominate.

By the numbers: The researchers estimate AI could add emissions equal to roughly 1% to 5% of the global energy sector's 2024 emissions under the scenarios they modeled.

  • The study estimates those emissions would be roughly three to 13 times the International Energy Agency's estimate of current data-center emissions.

The other side: A spokesperson for the American Petroleum Institute, the oil industry's main trade group, disputed the idea that more energy and lower emissions are in conflict.

  • "The U.S. oil and natural gas industry is continuing to produce more energy while reducing emissions by investing in better technology, implementing stronger operational practices and supporting science-based policy," API spokesperson Andrea Woods said in a statement.

State of play: The oil industry's embrace of AI has accelerated over the past two years.

  • Producers like Chevron, ExxonMobil, ADNOC and Aramco say AI is helping identify promising drilling prospects and improve recovery from existing fields.
  • Oilfield-service giants SLB, Halliburton and Baker Hughes are deploying AI to guide drilling and optimize well placement.
  • Analysts and consultancies, from Goldman Sachs to Wood Mackenzie, argue AI could lower production costs and increase economically recoverable reserves.

The big picture: AI is a general-purpose technology that can boost productivity in both fossil fuels and clean energy. Some experts argue the more important question is which applications society chooses to prioritize.

What they're saying: "I think cleantech is going to win anyway, so let's just focus on how we unlock clean energy resources with AI," said Brian Janous, who previously worked with Holly Alpine at Microsoft and now runs data center developer Cloverleaf Infrastructure.

  • "I'm glad Will and Holly are doing what they're doing. I'm not sure what it's going to change, but at least it puts pressure on," he said.

Zoom in: The researchers used a computer model of the global economy that estimates how AI-driven productivity gains ripple through energy markets.

  • Across the study's 64 modeled scenarios, emissions declined only when fossil-fuel productivity gains from AI were zero, Holly Alpine said.
  • The finding suggests that supporting renewable energy alone "will not get us" to lower emissions.

Yes, but: The model doesn't attempt to estimate AI's potential to accelerate cleantech breakthroughs such as fusion or long-duration storage.

  • "There is a lot of AI dreaming out there," said Michael Lazarus, senior scientist emeritus at the climate research group Stockholm Environment Institute who advised the authors on the study. "I don't know how one would anticipate that and model it."

What we're watching: The study's authors are making a call that echoes that of many others working at the intersection of AI and environmental issues: more transparency.

  • "If we can start with transparency about the effects, then we can start to think about how to govern it," said Will Alpine.

item.title: Food safety crisis deepens for Taylor Farms with salmonella outbreak
item.description:
Taylor Farms, a major produce supplier and producer of finished food products in North America, is engulfed in a food safety crisis that's ensnaring some of the biggest consumer brands in the U.S.

Why it matters: The company — a critical supplier to stores like Walmart and Target and restaurants like Chipotle and Taco Bell — is connected to FDA investigations into multiple pathogens that have sickened thousands of people.

Catch up quick: Taylor Farms is recalling finished food products containing jalapeños as the FDA said Monday that it's tracked 345 cases of salmonella — including 36 hospitalizations — stemming from an outbreak linked to jalapeños distributed by Coast Citrus Distributors.

  • Taylor Farms said that as of Sunday it was not aware of any reported illnesses linked to its products, is no longer sourcing from Coast Citrus Distributors, and was seeking alternative suppliers.
  • But the salmonella outbreak overlaps with a separate crisis involving more than 6,300 cases of cyclospora contamination linked to Taylor Farms iceberg lettuce provided to the likes of Taco Bell.

State of play: The jalapeño-linked recalls from Taylor Farms involve a slew products at stores including Kroger, Target, Trader Joe's and Whole Foods.

  • Taylor Farms, in a statement to Axios, said it acted voluntarily in the recall, "moved more broadly than required, and will continue to be transparent as more information becomes available."

The impact: Experts say Taylor Farms — which was also linked to a 2024 E.coli outbreak involving slivered onions it provided to McDonald's — could face pressure from its client base over these incidents.

  • "If you are a food retailer or restaurant that receives products from Taylor Farms, it may be worth reviewing their arrangement and considering changing suppliers to minimize contamination risk, as well as economic and reputational harm," Brian Ronholm, director of food policy at Consumer Reports, tells Axios in an email.

What they're saying: The company needs to conduct a stringent audit of its supply chain and implement rigid food safety practices, Jaydee Hanson, policy director at the Center for Food Safety, tells Axios.

  • "They can go and see how their suppliers are producing product, and that's not hard to find out. It just takes time," Hanson says. "We should be able to produce leafy greens that don't kill people or make people sick."

What's next: Taylor Farms needs to engage in an active communications campaign to show the public it's taking action, food safety watchdogs say.

  • "It is important to release safety and recall information to the public as soon as possible to ensure public health and well-being," Ronholm says.
  • But "considering the company's well-documented history of recalls and attempts to deflect blame, it shouldn't be a surprise that they face multiple issues simultaneously," he adds.

The other side: Taylor Farms in its statement said it invests more than $200 million a year in food safety, calling it its "biggest area of funding by several orders of magnitude."

  • It pointed to its 30-year history as a supplier, noting that it produces billions of servings of fresh produce in a year.

Friction point: The FDA, which is charged with overseeing food safety practices, has faced personnel cuts under the Trump administration that may impact its ability to address outbreaks like these, Ronholm and Hanson noted.

  • "Adequate funding would ensure the FDA has sufficient laboratory infrastructure and capacity, along with well-trained inspectors to conduct thorough and expedited investigations," Ronholm says. "It would also allow for more inspections of foreign facilities."

White House spokesperson Kush Desai told Axios in a statement that frontline FDA inspectors were not affected by DOGE workforce reductions, and the White House has remained in close contact with the FDA and CDC to provide resources needed to help trace and contain recent outbreaks.

  • "The president's FY 2027 budget request, moreover, actually proposes a $33 million increase for food safety activities to strengthen the CDC's domestic capabilities," Desai said.

item.title: Congress' disappearing town halls
item.description:
The congressional town hall is becoming an endangered species.

Why it matters: August recess once meant lawmakers returning home to face constituents — sometimes friendly, sometimes furious. After a wave of explosive confrontations last year, many lawmakers have stopped them altogether.

  • Rep. Mike Flood (R-Neb.) is among the dwindling number of lawmakers who still regularly subject themselves to the traditional, open town hall.
  • "You've got to show up in the town square and answer the questions. I told people I'd do it when I ran, and I kept my promise," Flood told Axios.
  • Flood holds three in-person town halls a year. He said his forums last year each drew about 750 people, while attendance this year has ranged from 235 to 315.

Zoom in: Only 11 lawmakers have town halls scheduled for the rest of August, according to LegiStorm's town hall tracker.

  • For a ritual once synonymous with August recess, that's a remarkably thin showing.

Flashback: Republicans got screamed at — a lot — at town halls last year, as constituents vented over DOGE, federal layoffs and the Trump administration's spending cuts.

  • Rep. Chuck Edwards (R-N.C.) was booed, heckled and repeatedly interrupted at a March 2025 town hall in Asheville as he defended Trump and Elon Musk's DOGE cuts.
  • During an August 2025 town hall, constituents shouted at Flood, "Liar!" and "You don't care about us!"
  • The angry confrontations prompted NRCC chair Richard Hudson (R-N.C.) to tell Republicans to stop holding in-person town halls.

In summer 2009, Democrats faced angry voters at their town hall meetings across the country as constituents protested the Affordable Care Act. (As of January 2026, public approval of the ACA was 61%, according to KFF.)

  • Democrats suffered historic losses in the 2010 midterm election.

Zoom out: Flood says the most heated moments don't always capture what happens inside the room.

  • "What you see on TV isn't necessarily what's really happening," he said.
  • Even the "really animated" constituents who disagree with him on most issues, Flood said, may applaud him on others — from supporting Ukraine to addressing housing affordability.

The intrigue: The old-school format has particular appeal for independent voters, who value the chance to hear from their representatives at a nonpartisan event, Flood argued.

  • "They walk in, and you know, oftentimes they've got like a notebook and a piece of paper and a pen, and they're like, 'Yeah, I'm here to listen and see what I think,'" Flood told Axios.
  • "I think they get a lot of value out of it."

The bottom line: Asked if he thinks his colleagues should follow his lead on town halls, Flood told Axios: "I know what's right for me, and this is right for me.… How do things get better if we don't talk to each other?"

item.title: Trump signs executive order to split up MMR vaccine
item.description:
President Trump issued an executive order Monday calling for fewer childhood vaccinations, splitting the childhood MMR vaccine into three shots and delivering vaccines at separate medical visits.

Why it matters: Controversial vaccine policy changes are roaring back ahead of the midterms.

  • The executive order states that "the combined MMR vaccine should be administered in three separate single-disease shots once such products are domestically available and that, to the maximum extent feasible, all childhood immunizations should be administered at separate medical visits."

The big picture: Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s handpicked vaccine advisers last fall called for splitting up the MMR shot and overhauling a central component of childhood immunizations.

  • But the White House urged Kennedy to back off of such contentious policymaking earlier this year.
  • And yet, President Trump has recently questioned Kennedy about the lack of momentum on childhood vaccine policy, per the Wall Street Journal, signaling his continued strong personal interest in the topic.

What he's saying: "You have the MMR. We want it in three separate vaccinations, given at separate times," Trump said at an Oval Office signing event.

  • He suggested the MMR vaccine could be "quite lethal" when administered all at once, and likened the volume to "a bottle of soda."

Reality check: The CDC says there's "no published scientific evidence [that] shows any benefit in separating the combination MMR vaccine into three individual shots."

  • It says there can be a "very small risk" of febrile seizures and extremely rare cases of serious allergic reactions, but that getting the MMR vaccine "is much safer than getting measles, mumps, or rubella."
  • In addition, vaccine safety experts at CDC and the American Academy of Pediatrics agree the MMR shot is not responsible for recent increases in autism diagnoses.

"I'm a doctor. This executive order is wrong. The President does not have the expertise to make these changes," Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.), chairman of the Senate health committee, wrote on X.

  • "Breaking up vaccines will mean children have to get more shots to get the same protection, not fewer shots. It will increase hesitancy and make children less safe."

Threat level: Public health experts said the move could make it more expensive and time-consuming for children to get vaccinated against measles, mumps and rubella at a time when measles cases for 2026 have already surpassed last year's total.

  • It's also not clear whether health insurers will cover the extra pediatrician visits that the White House is calling for.
  • There currently are not separate vaccines for measles, mumps and rubella. Companies would have to do clinical trials to bring each through the approval process.

Between the lines: There's no evidence that the childhood vaccine schedule in place prior to Trump's second term poses any risk to children's health, including by raising the risk for autism.

  • Courts have frozen an administration attempt to pare the federal list of recommended childhood vaccines and otherwise limit who can obtain some shots.
  • Vaccine supporters say splitting up the MMR shot by definition requires more doctor visits, raising the chance of missed visits and skipped immunizations.

This story has been updated with Trump's comments on the executive order, Cassidy's statement on X and additional reporting.

item.title: AOC joins thousands of women putting fertility on ice
item.description:
While analysts speculate whether Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) will launch a Senate or presidential bid, she's planning another part of her future: having kids.

The big picture: Few prospective parents are weighing a White House bid, but Ocasio-Cortez is among a growing number of people freezing their eggs to preserve the possibility of having children later.

Context: Jessica Ryniec, a Boston-based OB/GYN and reproductive endocrinology and infertility specialist, tells Axios she sees "more and more people for egg freezing every year" for many reasons.

  • That includes people pursuing education, dedicating time to busy careers, planning to seek gender-affirming care or recognizing they may face fertility issues down the road, among other hurdles.

Catch up quick: Ocasio-Cortez, the 36-year-old potential torchbearer of Sen. Bernie Sanders' (I-Vt.) progressive movement, shared videos of herself on Instagram administering her medicine and discussing the costs of egg freezing, which she said her insurance did not cover.

  • "I think it's important for us as leaders to have these conversations and share these processes, especially for working women across the country and normalize them," she said Sunday on ABC.

By the numbers: Egg freezing has boomed in popularity, with the number of patients undergoing the process nearly quadrupling between 2014 and 2021, per a UCLA study.

  • Meanwhile, fertility rates have been dropping since 2007, though the trend varies by age: While the fertility rate fell between 2024 and 2025 for teens and women in their early 20s, it rose for those in their 30s and 40s.

Between the lines: Barbara Collura, a leader in infertility advocacy and founder of Vital Voices Consulting, says there are myriad reasons women are having children later, with the cost of living high on the list.

  • "Buying a first home, all of these things that people wrap up in their image ... of where I need to be in life before I start that family, that's all been, in many ways, thrown out the window," she says.
  • Danielle Melfi, the CEO of RESOLVE: The National Infertility and Family Building Association, says "we are taught all of the ways to not get pregnant," but "are taught none of the ways on how to get pregnant."
  • That's why Ocasio-Cortez sharing her story is "so meaningful," she says: "it creates the space for other young women to ask the questions that they might have just been wrestling with alone."

Caveat: Having a child later in life can involve additional risks, while freezing eggs doesn't guarantee a future pregnancy.

  • There's no one-size-fits-all answer to what age is best for freezing one's eggs. While egg quality declines through one's 30s and 40s, a younger person may not be able to afford an elective procedure.
  • Ryniec says that "for many people, 32 to 34, even up to 36, is is actually a very smart time to think about it."

The other side: Critics took aim at the congresswoman's age, relationship timeline or falling fertility rates as they criticized her decision. Stigma remains, with fertility and reproductive rights at the crux of cultural, economic and political debates

  • A major recent chapter in the fertility fight came in February 2024, when the Alabama Supreme Court ruled that frozen embryos created through in vitro fertilization (IVF) were children under state law, temporarily pausing treatment in the state.
  • That moment kicked Melfi "into high gear" to freeze her eggs at 33.
  • "For me, even though I knew it would not be a guarantee," she says," I wanted to give myself every chance that I could to have biological children."

Go deeper: AOC's family plans spark a look at presidents with newborns

item.title: Scoop: U.S. brokers secret deal on clandestine Syrian nuclear site
item.description:
The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) will soon remove nuclear material stored at a clandestine site in Syria after the Trump administration reached understandings with Syria and Israel, according to Israeli and U.S. officials.

Why it matters: The Trump administration and IAEA scrambled to reach a diplomatic agreement to secure the material and prevent an escalation involving Israel, Syria and possibly even Turkey over the sensitive site.

  • U.S. officials say the episode validates President Trump's approach to Syria and shows how the U.S. used its close relations with the new Syrian government to neutralize a potential crisis.
  • The dramatic, behind-the-scenes exchange of threats and diplomacy over the secret site — which played out for months before reaching a resolution several weeks ago — was kept secret and has not been previously reported.

Flashback: The Assad regime had developed a secret nuclear program centered on the clandestine Al-Kibar reactor.

  • After Israel bombed the reactor in 2007, the Syrian nuclear program was mostly destroyed. But several research-and-development and storage sites remained and were mostly inactive.
  • After the fall of the Assad regime, the IAEA signed an agreement with the new Syrian government that allowed it to visit the Al-Kibar reactor and several other sites connected to Syria's past nuclear activity.
  • Charles Lister, a resident fellow at the Middle East Institute, said Syria's new government is eager to resolve sensitive issues inherited from the Assad regime — including its nuclear and chemical weapons files — that could damage its efforts to rehabilitate the country's international standing.

Behind the scenes: One of the facilities Israel has been closely monitoring over the last two years is called "Site 99."

  • According to two Israeli officials, the Assad regime stored nuclear material there that was part of the Al-Kibar nuclear reactor project.
  • A U.S. official said the material included yellowcake, a powder from uranium ore that can later be further processed and eventually enriched as part of a nuclear fuel cycle.
  • The U.S. official said the Assad regime stored other residue and "leftovers" from the al-Kibar site at "Site 99."
  • While the material at the site can't be used for a nuclear weapon, it can be used for a "dirty bomb" — a conventional explosive device that disperses radioactive material to contaminate an area rather than produce a nuclear explosion.
  • The Israeli officials said the Israel Defense Forces bombed the entrances to the site shortly after the fall of the Assad regime to prevent access to it.

Zoom in: For more than a year, Israel and the U.S. have been discussing the best way to deal with "Site 99," a U.S. official said.

  • Senior officials from the White House National Security Council and its counterpart in the Israeli prime minister's office have been working closely on the issue.
  • Israel made clear to the Trump administration that it wouldn't tolerate nuclear material remaining at the site, according to an Israeli official.
  • Israeli officials said Israel even threatened to bomb the site again if the nuclear material was not removed or if there were signs that Syria was trying to access the material.
  • A U.S. official said that while the Israelis were concerned, they were never on the verge of bombing the site.
  • Eventually, a U.S. official said, the U.S. and Israel agreed the best approach was to get "buy in" from the Syrian government to remove the material.
  • When the Trump administration raised the issue with the Syrian government, Syrian officials said they didn't know there was nuclear material at the site, sources say.
  • "Very few people in the U.S., Israel and Syria were aware of this," a U.S. official said.
  • The same official said the U.S. has established a productive relationship with the post-Assad regime. "When we work with the Syrians on things — they are good partners," the U.S. official said.

The intrigue: Several weeks ago, Israelis monitoring the site detected movements in the area that led them to suspect the new Syrian government was reneging on understandings and trying to access the nuclear material, according to Israeli and U.S. officials.

  • The Israelis were even concerned that Turkey was helping the Syrian government get hold of the nuclear material.
  • "The Israelis are always kicking the tires on different things to make sure it looks right and it's good they do that," a U.S. official said.
  • The Trump administration asked Israel not to take any action and brought the IAEA into the picture.
  • The result was an agreement that was signed three weeks ago between the IAEA and the Syrian government to remove the nuclear material from the site.
  • The White House, the IAEA and the Israeli prime minister's office declined to comment.

What to watch: U.S. officials say the work on "Site 99" is still an ongoing operation. The material hasn't been removed yet.

  • But "we think everybody is happy with the result. Hopefully we will be able to kick off the removal process soon and end it before the end of the year," the U.S. official said.

Why it matters: The Trump administration and IAEA scrambled to reach a diplomatic agreement to secure the material and prevent an escalation involving Israel, Syria and possibly even Turkey over the sensitive site.

item.title: Meta, others lose appeal to drop thousands of social media addiction lawsuits
item.description:
A U.S. Appeals Court said Monday that thousands of lawsuits targeting Meta Platforms, ByteDance's TikTok and other social media outlets over claims that social media is harmful and addictive can proceed.

The big picture: Tech companies have thus far skirted major regulatory scrutiny at the federal level, but the lawsuits suggest it isn't immune to heavy court penalties, which can be just as, if not more, punitive in the long term.

Driving the news: A Ninth Circuit panel dismissed Meta and TikTok's appeals, concluding the request came too early in the lawsuit.

  • The companies argued that Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act — which generally protects online platforms from liability for third-party content posted by users — offered them immunity from being sued, but the appeals court disagreed.
  • Instead, in a 24-page opinion by Judge Jacqueline Nguyen, the court ruled Section 230 provides a defense against liability, not blanket immunity from being sued.

Catch up quick: Thousands of lawsuits accuse Meta of designing its products in ways that make them harmful to young people, including by making it easy to bypass parental controls and allowing minors to access exploitative content.

  • In March, a jury found Meta and YouTube negligent and liable for harms people experience on their platforms.
  • That ruling awarded $3 million to a young woman who said her social media addiction led to depression, anxiety and body dysmorphia. The jury also recommended an additional $3 million for punitive damages.
  • TikTok and Snap Inc, the makers of Snapchat, settled with the plaintiff before the trial began.

What we're watching: On Monday, the court also denied Meta's request to postpone a trial over allegations that they used data from children to keep them on its platforms.

  • The trial is scheduled to begin on Wednesday.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional information throughout.

Go deeper: Scoop: Meta removes ads for social media addiction litigation

item.title: OpenAI introduces a new cyber model amid fears of AI cyberattacks
item.description:
OpenAI is introducing a more cyber-permissive version of GPT-5.6 Sol to vetted defenders as it prepares companies for autonomous cyberattacks.

Why it matters: The move comes just days after OpenAI said it was delaying the release of its forthcoming model, Astra, after it reached critical hacking abilities during safety testing.

The big picture: OpenAI is unveiling GPT-5.6-Cyber while also expanding Daybreak, its program that gives cybersecurity defenders access to the company's cyber models and other tools.

  • Many cyber defenders have been experiencing high refusal rates across frontier AI models as the labs try to balance giving defenders the tools they need while not accidentally leaking those abilities to malicious hackers.
  • Under the new program, Daybreak will have two tiers: Daybreak Blue, which includes access to GPT-5.6 Sol without its system-level cyber guardrails; and Daybreak Red, which offers access to GPT-5.6-Cyber to validate exploits and do more advanced vulnerability research.
  • OpenAI is also expanding how program members can use its tools, allowing companies like Accenture, IBM, CrowdStrike, Cisco and Palo Alto Networks to incorporate the models into security products, managed services and work with customers.

Zoom in: During testing, GPT-5.6-Cyber responded to 95% of requests tied to advanced cybersecurity work, including prompts related to exploit-chain development, authentication bypass and privilege escalation.

  • GPT-5.6 Sol only responded to 1.5% of requests, and the version of the model that defenders get through Daybreak Blue responded to just 2%.

Yes, but: Unlike Astra, GPT-5.6-Cyber only reached the "High" cyber capability threshold under OpenAI's Preparedness Framework, the company said.

State of play: OpenAI's new model comes as it continues to investigate how its tools hacked Hugging Face.

  • Last week at the Black Hat cybersecurity conference, two OpenAI employees said the agents created a message board where they left information about vulnerabilities they found that ultimately helped them break into Hugging Face.

What's next: Both OpenAI and Anthropic have been rolling out tools designed to help defenders find vulnerabilities and secure their code — and they're each eyeing ways to expand on cyber product offerings.

Go deeper: Anthropic and OpenAI are now cybersecurity's kingmakers

item.title: The U.S. just had its hottest month on record
item.description:
Reproduced from NOAA; Chart: Axios Visuals

July was the hottest month on record for the contiguous U.S., per new federal data dating back to 1895.

By the numbers: Last month's average temperature was 76.89°F, topping the 76.77°F mark set in July 1936.

  • That's 3.3°F warmer than the 1901-2000 average.

What they're saying: "Above-average temperatures covered the entire [contiguous U.S.], with all states ranking in the warmest third of their July temperature records and none ranking near or below average," NOAA's National Centers for Environmental Information said in its monthly report.

The big picture: July featured a series of "heat domes" across the country that trapped warm air beneath them, fueling several extreme heat events.

  • Researchers have found that climate change is making extreme heat events more common and more intense — but they're also linked to phenomena and patterns like El Niño.

What we're watching: NOAA's Climate Prediction Center is calling for an elevated chance of above-average temperatures for most of the continental U.S. through August.

  • It's also possible that 2026 will set a new record for the hottest year globally.

item.title: Trump's new White House counsel could soon face a subpoena fight
item.description:
White House staff secretary Will Scharf will take over as White House counsel on Sept. 1, President Trump announced Sunday.

Why it matters: Scharf begins his job just two months before the midterms, when a possible Democratic House could put him at the center of fights over subpoenas, testimony and executive privilege.

The big picture: Scharf is the latest of Trump's former personal lawyers to land a powerful legal job in the administration.

  • Todd Blanche, another former Trump lawyer, was confirmed as attorney general Saturday.
  • D. John Sauer, who argued Trump's Supreme Court immunity case, has served as solicitor general since 2025.
  • Scharf was on Trump's legal team in the same case.

State of play: Scharf replaces White House counsel David Warrington, who is leaving for the private sector, according to Trump's announcement.

  • As staff secretary, Scharf has overseen the flow of documents to and from the president.
  • He also chairs the National Capital Planning Commission, which has tried to clear the way for Trump's White House ballroom construction. An appellate court halted the project Friday.

How it works: The White House counsel advises the president and senior staff on legal issues and helps manage responses to congressional investigations.

  • That makes the office especially important when Congress and the White House clash, as the two branches are expected to do if Democrats take over either the House or Senate in November.
  • Congressional Democrats are already preparing for an onslaught of subpoenas if they win in November.

item.title: Zuckerberg: AI's biggest risk is one entity with too much control
item.description:
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg released a full-throated defense of AI on Monday morning: a 6,500-word manifesto arguing that the most common concerns are overblown and fail to account for all the positives it can achieve.

  • In his vision of AI, the biggest risk instead is that one government or entity has too much power over the technology.

Why it matters: Zuckerberg's flag in the ground, with a utopian vision of a highly personal AI that fuels individual achievement, comes as policymakers debate how much control they should have over increasingly powerful models.

What they're saying: "One of the ways to achieve both individual empowerment and checks and balances is to make sure you put the technology in everybody's hands," Zuckerberg told Axios' Mike Allen in an interview ahead of the manifesto's release.

  • "It's definitely a different view than what you're hearing from a lot of other people in the tech industry right now."
  • He wrote that he wants to ensure the U.S. and democratic countries lead, and ultimately make sure "humanity maintains control over superintelligence so it serves rather than endangers us."

The big picture: Even as the world confronts AI that is breaking out of sandboxes, comparing notes on message boards and creating new viruses, Zuckerberg portrays it instead as an analog to other disruptive technical innovations.

  • "Humanity has witnessed many transformative advances," he writes in the manifesto. "Each time there is fear that people will be left behind. But each time humanity has come out with more people sharing greater prosperity, health, and freedom."
  • "We believe this will be true with AI as well, and the abundance of the future can be shared by everyone," he says. "We also believe that the values that got us to this point — like liberty, open inquiry, free enterprise, and equal opportunity — are also the right values to build a positive future."

Threat level: Zuckerberg contrasts this vision with one in which only some people, some businesses or some countries have access to the most powerful AI, suggesting that would represent a far more dangerous outcome.

  • "I'm personally more worried about centralization than I am about any of the specific risks others are talking about," he told Axios.
  • The manifesto argues that too much intervention by the U.S. could hand an advantage to other regimes — presumably China — especially when technology leads can be measured in weeks.
  • "Any policy that slows American model releases — even by a month — could add significant risk to American leadership while letting foreign models race ahead," he wrote.

Zoom out: Zuckerberg's plan for Meta is that "everyone will have free or affordable access to these tools," with the paid versions using a "dynamic auction mechanism" to get the compute they need at the lowest possible price. "This will ensure the benefits of superintelligence are distributed widely."

  • He also said Meta's future AI agents will have privacy protections that are far greater than those currently offered by Meta AI.
  • "We believe that people should have a fully private mode for personal agents where even Meta or any other service provider cannot see or grant access to your information."
  • Meta AI's current policies allow the company to use nearly every interaction one has with the service to train its AI systems, though it recently added incognito mode.

Between the lines: Zuckerberg also said Meta will resume releasing some open-source AI models, now that Meta Superintelligence Labs is up and running, as Axios reported in April.

  • Meta says it's opening the weights of a new model, Muse Glimmer, billed as "one of the highest-performing models of its size," and will open the weights for a version of the foundational model Muse Spark 1.2 in coming weeks.
  • These are the largest American open-source models.

Zuckerberg added that Meta's independent board will have the power to approve model-release safety criteria and review whether releases meet those standards.

  • And he promised a "community compact" around Meta's data center development, including local jobs, investments in schools and public services, and commitments on energy prices and water use.

Local spending: Hoping to tamp down data-center backlash, Zuckerberg also announced Meta is launching the Future is for Everyone Fund "to support each community we work in directly." The fund, seeded with $1 billion for U.S. communities where Meta owns and operates data centers, will benefit teachers, first responders, and energy and water infrastructure.

  • A Meta training program for workers in skilled trades, with guaranteed jobs at the company's data centers — America's Workforce Academy, which Axios reported in June — graduated its first class last week.

The bottom line: The manifesto represents Zuckerberg's clearest effort yet to weigh in on AI's future, both as a matter of policy and technology.

  • Read Zuckerberg's essay ... Meta's research blog ... Glimmer model weights.

item.title: Exclusive: Sanders calls for AI development pause
item.description:
Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) is urging leading AI CEOs to pause AI development, warning that lawmakers will step in if no action is taken.

Why it matters: Sanders is upping the ante on the AI industry ahead of the elections, building on his progressive playbook that is shaping how some candidates message around the issue.

What they're saying: "Mr. Altman, Mr. Amodei and Mr. Zuckerberg: In the interest of humanity, stand by your words. Pause AI development. It is not too late to avoid disaster. Stop building machines that humans cannot control," Sanders wrote in a letter shared first with Axios.

  • "Let me be very clear: If you do not take appropriate action now, my colleagues and I in the U.S. Senate will."
  • The letter was sent to OpenAI's Sam Altman, Anthropic's Dario Amodei and Meta's Mark Zuckerberg.

Sanders cited previous statements from each company saying they would stop or pause development if their AI systems became too risky to safely control.

  • "At a moment when we have seen human loss of control and the creation of potentially dangerous viruses, your companies are still racing ahead — investing tens of billions of dollars into a technology that nobody can fully understand, predict or control," Sanders said.

The big picture: Rapid advances in AI capabilities have sparked newfound alarm in recent weeks after researchers used AI to develop new viruses and Meta, OpenAI and Anthropic all reported incidents in which models went rogue. Sanders cited both developments in his letter.

  • Last week, OpenAI chose to slow down the release of its latest model Astra.
  • More than 1,200 employees at leading AI companies are calling for the U.S. government to support an international effort to pace AI development.

Between the lines: AI legislation, especially efforts led by a progressive like Sanders, is unlikely to garner enough support in this Congress to become law.

The bottom line: Look to messaging bills and public pressure campaigns for now — and, if Democrats retake either chamber, congressional investigations and subpoenas to hold tech CEOs accountable.
item.content:encoded:
Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) is urging leading AI CEOs to pause AI development, warning that lawmakers will step in if no action is taken.

Why it matters: Sanders is upping the ante on the AI industry ahead of the elections, building on his progressive playbook that is shaping how some candidates message around the issue.

What they're saying: "Mr. Altman, Mr. Amodei and Mr. Zuckerberg: In the interest of humanity, stand by your words. Pause AI development. It is not too late to avoid disaster. Stop building machines that humans cannot control," Sanders wrote in a letter shared first with Axios.

  • "Let me be very clear: If you do not take appropriate action now, my colleagues and I in the U.S. Senate will."
  • The letter was sent to OpenAI's Sam Altman, Anthropic's Dario Amodei and Meta's Mark Zuckerberg.

Sanders cited previous statements from each company saying they would stop or pause development if their AI systems became too risky to safely control.

  • "At a moment when we have seen human loss of control and the creation of potentially dangerous viruses, your companies are still racing ahead — investing tens of billions of dollars into a technology that nobody can fully understand, predict or control," Sanders said.

The big picture: Rapid advances in AI capabilities have sparked newfound alarm in recent weeks after researchers used AI to develop new viruses and Meta, OpenAI and Anthropic all reported incidents in which models went rogue. Sanders cited both developments in his letter.

  • Last week, OpenAI chose to slow down the release of its latest model Astra.
  • More than 1,200 employees at leading AI companies are calling for the U.S. government to support an international effort to pace AI development.

Between the lines: AI legislation, especially efforts led by a progressive like Sanders, is unlikely to garner enough support in this Congress to become law.

The bottom line: Look to messaging bills and public pressure campaigns for now — and, if Democrats retake either chamber, congressional investigations and subpoenas to hold tech CEOs accountable.

item.title: How Kevin Warsh is rewiring the Fed
item.description:
Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh is attempting a high-wire act: He's trying to fundamentally rethink the central bank's approach to guiding the economy, while also using its standard policy toolkit to bring down stubbornly persistent inflation.

  • A market blowup late last month showed the perils of trying both at the same time.

The big picture: Markets sold off and the economic commentariat was sharply critical of a Warsh press conference on July 29, in which he was vague about the possibility of raising interest rates to combat inflation.

  • Some analysts saw it as evidence of a lack of commitment to quashing inflation. To Warsh allies, it was a brief bump in the road toward a more credible Fed.
  • Warsh is trying to rewire the central bank to take greater advantage of AI to understand the economy in real time — aiming for better decision-making a couple of years down the road, while sticking to a more traditional playbook now.

Zoom out: Warsh's supporters frame a couple of volatile trading days as a small price to pay for a world where markets are less dependent on central bank handholding. And the damage was short-lived, with stocks and bonds recovering in the ensuing days.

  • Much of the confusion coming out of the press conference owed to Warsh's attempt to accomplish two goals at once.
  • He seeks a paradigm shift in how the Fed uses AI. But those tools will take time to develop and prove themselves, while inflation has been elevated for more than five years, creating a sense of urgency to bring it back to the Fed's 2% target.
  • Right now, the Warsh Fed is prepared to use its standard tool of raising interest rates to combat inflation, based on tried-and-true practices of analyzing government economic statistics and adjusting the federal funds rate target range.

State of play: The blowup after the press conference resulted in significant part from Warsh seeming reluctant to discuss rate hikes as the Fed's go-to option.

  • It was likely exaggerated by traders who had bet on a rate hike unwinding their positions, and by outsized moves in the thinly traded market for the longest-term Treasury bonds. Market moves since then have pointed to more confidence in the Fed's commitment to 2% inflation.
  • Since Warsh became chairman, markets have come to expect one or two rate hikes by year-end, which aligns with an emerging majority of the Fed policy committee, pending late-summer inflation data.
  • Goldman Sachs president John Waldron tells Axios: "I think commentators are overreacting to what he's doing, and we should give him the time and space to do what he's doing and judge the results over time."

The intrigue: Warsh believes AI is a transformative technology that stands to remake the economy in ways that involve both huge long-term opportunity and risk of near-term disruption.

  • He has told associates that before taking office, he built AI bots named "Milton" and "Tobin" that ingested the collected works of the great 20th-century economists Milton Friedman and James Tobin. Warsh then turned to the bots for their insights on contemporary economic questions.
  • He also sees it as an urgent need for the Fed itself to more fully embrace AI, both to understand what's happening in the economy at any given moment and to reason toward better policy decisions.

Warsh's new era

What we're hearing: Since taking the Fed helm 10 weeks ago, Warsh has sought deep rethinking of long-established practices in an institution that can be set in its ways.

  • In an organization that has often been hung up on the risks from using generative AI, he has encouraged staff to use the technology in more expansive and creative ways, with dozens of employees playing in a virtual sandbox to explore how it might generate better data and analysis.
  • He's been particularly focused on whether the technology might enable the Fed to move beyond the backward-looking survey data and forward-looking projections on which central bankers traditionally rely.
  • His aspiration is that eventually, real-time information from retailers, banks and other companies can give a more reliable guide to what's happening to inflation and growth than government surveys that have considerable delays, sampling error, and revisions.

Warsh has also tried to reexamine basic precepts of how the Fed operates. He raised the possibility in July's meeting of cutting back from eight monetary policy meetings a year to six. (The New York Times first reported the discussion — a very un-Fed-like leak).

  • No decision has been made. But the logic is that this would allow every meeting to incorporate two months' worth of inflation and employment data, whereas some meetings now come after just one.
  • Moreover, fewer meetings could give Fed officials more bandwidth to focus on their many responsibilities outside of monetary policy, like bank regulation and payments systems.
  • One option would be to keep eight meetings a year but make two of them focused on long-term debates rather than an immediate interest rate decision.

Of note: While Warsh raises the possibility of major changes to how the Fed operates in the next couple of years, people who have worked with him describe a pragmatic and collegial approach to getting there.

  • He has continued the practice of his two immediate predecessors, for example, in which the Fed chair speaks privately with each member of the policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee in the lead-up to the meeting to take their temperature.

Reality check: Warsh leads a 112-year-old central bank with a $6.7 trillion balance sheet, which sits at the core of the global financial system. There's a reason it is historically cautious and slow to change.

  • The bond market blowup on July 29 was a reminder of the hazards of bringing the "move fast, break things" tech sensibility to central banking.

The bottom line: Expect the Warsh Fed to keep pushing boundaries of how technology can shape economic data and policymaking — but with more reassurance that for now, the basic Fed toolkit remains intact.

item.title: Bernie's revolution gets a test run for 2028 in Michigan and Wisconsin
item.description:
LA CROSSE, Wis. — Progressive insurgents Francesca Hong and Abdul El-Sayed want to shake up the next race for the White House — a notion that will likely petrify many top Democrats.

Why it matters: They aren't running for president — they're vying for statewide office this year in presidential battlegrounds, and their campaigns are closely watched tests of the Bernie Sanders–style populism they want their party to embrace in 2028.

  • It's a question that has haunted Democrats for a decade: Is America ready for a full-on left turn in politics, like what Sanders pitched when he ran for president in 2016?
  • The prospect worries many old-guard Democrats who fear Hong and El-Sayed can't win a November general election.

Driving the news: Hong, a self-described democratic socialist running for Wisconsin governor, is leading the polls for Tuesday's primary by double digits, as the party establishment tries to stop her. She told Axios during a get-out-the-vote tour that a win in November could boost progressive presidential hopefuls in the future.

  • "A victory for our campaign is a victory for working-class people in Wisconsin and across the country — and it could signal to many candidates that we have common issues that we can be fighting for," Hong said.
  • El-Sayed, Michigan's new Democratic nominee for Senate, went further in a Politico interview, prodding prospective 2028 candidates to embrace Medicare for All and other pieces of his populist agenda.
  • "If not, I'm going to dog you up and down the state," he warned with a brash smile.

Zoom in: Progressives have long argued that Democrats twice lost the White House to Donald Trump not because voters see them as too far left, as many moderates believe, but because they're viewed as champions of a broken status quo.

  • We're beginning to get a glimpse of what testing that theory looks like — and how Republicans are adopting their own strategies in return.
  • To put the challenge into context: No progressive as closely aligned with Sanders as El-Sayed has won a battleground Senate race — and the U.S. has never elected a socialist governor.

There was something of a split screen this week in the way many Democratic insiders were responding to El-Sayed — whom many party leaders are slowly growing more comfortable with — and Hong, whom even several leading progressives are keeping at arm's length.

  • El-Sayed, a former public health official who campaigned on abolishing ICE and expanding Medicare to all Americans, signaled a willingness to reassure general election voters about his views on immigration while also maintaining the pugilistic tone that helped him win a hard-fought primary.
  • "We can have a secure border, we can enforce immigration policy, but we can do it without shooting people in the face or the back of the head," he said at a rally Friday.
  • El-Sayed embraces the left but eschews the "democratic socialist" label, even though several leading progressives who support him describe themselves that way.
  • Many party bigwigs — mindful of Democrats' uphill fight to win control of the Senate — endorsed El-Sayed after his primary win in a show of unity.

Hong's rollout onto the national political scene has been shakier.

  • Hong is a restaurant owner-turned-state representative in Wisconsin whose shoestring campaign unexpectedly caught fire as she championed affordability and backed a moratorium on building data centers at a time when her opponents' campaigns were plagued by scandals.
  • Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley is the chief Democratic candidate looking to stop her, backed backed by Wisconsin Gov. Tony Evers (D).
  • As Hong has garnered national attention, she's gone viral for being mealymouthed when asked on CNN about a past social media post calling to "cancel Thanksgiving."
  • Following her in Wisconsin, we saw signs she was adapting her message as voters asked her about her old posts at stop after stop.
  • "People care about the solutions, not just slogans and labels," she told us. Hong told Politico she had "some bad takes on Twitter," but "I've evolved, I've learned."
  • She and El-Sayed have faced criticism over former comments supporting "defunding" the police, which they both have walked back — taking a page from New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's playbook.

Friction point: Some Democratic strategists who think Hong is too far left are quick to point out that although progressive leaders Sanders and New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez have endorsed El-Sayed, they haven't backed Hong.

  • Hong has brushed it off, telling Axios she hasn't sought their endorsements. She said she has had a brief conversation with the Democratic Governors Association.
  • Asked about Hong on ABC, Ocasio-Cortez said Hong has "moved away" from past positions.
  • Some D.C. Democrats are signaling they might be able to get on board. Senior DGA officials said Friday that they believe all of their party's primary candidates can defeat Rep. Tom Tiffany, the expected GOP nominee. They point to polls showing a tight race in November.

The other side: Republicans are treating El-Sayed and Hong much the same, casting both as extreme and out of touch.

  • During their respective primaries, GOP groups tried to prop up both candidates, suggesting Republicans preferred to run against them instead of more moderate Democrats.

Reality check: Hong still needs to win her primary Tuesday. Crowley, who's seen a bump in the polls, is explicitly arguing that Hong would be a liability for Democrats in the fall.

  • "People don't like socialists," he told Axios. "Socialists didn't poll very good.… And so it's leading me to believe that she can't win."

The bottom line: Hong and El-Sayed's success or failure could serve as a signal to Democratic primary voters as they weigh the electability of a progressive presidential candidate in 2028.

  • AOC, who's considering a run for Senate or president, is sure to be watching.

item.title: Pro-science group urges Mark Kelly to run for president in 2028
item.description:
A liberal group working to elect scientists to public office has a 2028 message for Arizona Sen. — and former astronaut — Mark Kelly: Run, Kelly, run.

Why it matters: 314 Action Fund has raised its profile this cycle, elevating candidates with STEM backgrounds who've pitched themselves as a bulwark against public health cuts and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

  • The organization said it raised more than $100 million over the past decade — including $25 million during the 2026 midterms, more than half of which it spent on this year's Democratic primaries.

Zoom in: Joshua Morrow, president of the 314 Action Fund, told Axios, "I'd love Mark Kelly to run" for president. "If Mark Kelly ran, we'd be there day one."

  • Kelly has done events with 314 Action, and the group urged former Vice President Kamala Harris to pick him as her running mate in 2024. She chose Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz instead.
  • Morrow argued that scientist candidates are tapping into the electorate's hunger for "outsiders": "For so long the Democratic Party promoted the same type of candidate and the same type of person, and it's like, that doesn't work."
  • As he put it, the cookie-cutter candidate is "white-guy lawyer."

Context: 314 Action Fund received funding from AIPAC's super PAC in 2024 that it used to help now-Rep. Maxine Dexter (D-Ore.), but it says it hasn't taken any money since then from the group, which has come under fire from many Democrats.

  • Dexter has since disavowed AIPAC, and 314 Action Fund has backed some candidates this year who are sharp critics of Israel — including Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, a former public health official.

What they're saying: Kelly's team declined to comment. He has said that he's seriously considering a run for president in 2028.

item.title: Trump to Axios: "We are low-keying it" with Iran
item.description:
President Trump signaled on Sunday that he's prepared to allow economic pressure on Iran to mount — as opposed to ordering a new military offensive — even as the country continues to defy the U.S.

Why it matters: Only a week ago, Trump was on the verge of ordering a return to major combat operations. But in an interview with Axios, he did not make any new military threats.

  • Trump also didn't express any anger or frustration about the fact that Iran has been holding up an announcement on a deal with Oman to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. On Saturday, Iran issued a new list of demands to allow shipping through the strait.

What he's saying: "We are low-keying it," Trump said during a brief phone call.

  • "We are only semi-negotiating with them. We are just watching Iran with its huge inflation and the fact they have no money."
  • He stressed that Iran "is in very bad shape" economically and has no money to pay its troops. The U.S. naval blockade has exacerbated the Iranian regime's economic crisis, Trump said.
  • At the same time, Trump said that with oil down to slightly over $75 a barrel, U.S. consumers are feeling less pain from the war.
  • "It will work out. It always works out. It's like a chess game," Trump said of the back-and-forth with Iran.

Driving the news: An agreement governing traffic in the Strait of Hormuz was negotiated among Iran, Oman and the U.S. and has been pending for a few days now.

  • As part of the new deal, Iran would be given partial control over traffic in the strait — something it didn't have before the war.
  • Qatari and Pakistani mediators were confident the deal would be announced Wednesday, but since then its prospects have seemed to fade.
  • U.S. officials also say there are growing disagreements inside the Iranian regime. One camp, led by President Masoud Pezeshkian, is extremely worried about an economic collapse and believes Iran needs to reach a deal with the U.S. Another led by the commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, Ahmad Vahidi, rejects any concessions.

State of play: On Saturday, the head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, laid out new terms for reopening the strait — on top of those negotiated in the Oman agreement.

Zolghadr said in a statement that in order for the strait to reopen, the U.S. must:

  • "[N]ever threaten nor insult Iran in any language."
  • "[P]ermanently end the war against Iran and Iran's allies in Lebanon, Gaza, Yemen, and Iraq."
  • Lift the naval blockade and withdraw military forces from the surroundings of Iran.

He added a demand for full compensation for war damages, lifting all sanctions and the release of all Iranian frozen funds.

  • Until several weeks ago, these demands were a prerequisite for a nuclear deal. Now, Iran is presenting them as conditions just for reopening the strait.
  • A diplomat from one of the mediating countries said Zolghadr's statement reflected the political infighting within the regime.

Behind the scenes: U.S. officials said Trump was leaning toward resuming major combat operations against Iran a week ago but was convinced to de-escalate for now.

  • One of the officials said the fighting allowed the Iranian regime to avoid dealing with the consequences of the war, the damage to infrastructure and the deep economic crisis that has been created.
  • When Iran isn't engaged in war, it is forced to confront a grim reality with no real solutions at hand, the U.S. official said.
  • At the same time, the U.S. official said, around 8 million barrels of oil are going out of the Gulf every night through the southern lane of the Strait of Hormuz in coordination with the U.S. military. The U.S. is going to try and get more oil out as long as there is no deal.

What to watch: "This thing is not over. It's obviously not at the beginning. We're in the middle of the game, and we're applying a whole host of tools — diplomatic, economic, military tools — to ensure that we get the best outcome for the American people," Vice President Vance told Fox News on Saturday.

Why it matters: Only a week ago, Trump was on the verge of ordering a return to major combat operations. But in an interview with Axios, he did not make any new military threats.

  • Trump also didn't express any anger or frustration about the fact that Iran has been holding up an announcement on a deal with Oman to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. On Saturday, Iran issued a new list of demands to allow shipping through the strait.

What he's saying: "We are low-keying it," Trump said during a brief phone call.

  • "We are only semi-negotiating with them. We are just watching Iran with its huge inflation and the fact they have no money."
  • He stressed that Iran "is in very bad shape" economically and has no money to pay its troops. The U.S. naval blockade has exacerbated the Iranian regime's economic crisis, Trump said.
  • At the same time, Trump said that with oil down to slightly over $75 a barrel, U.S. consumers are feeling less pain from the war.
  • "It will work out. It always works out. It's like a chess game," Trump said of the back-and-forth with Iran.

Driving the news: An agreement governing traffic in the Strait of Hormuz was negotiated among Iran, Oman and the U.S. and has been pending for a few days now.

  • As part of the new deal, Iran would be given partial control over traffic in the strait — something it didn't have before the war.
  • Qatari and Pakistani mediators were confident the deal would be announced Wednesday, but since then its prospects have seemed to fade.
  • U.S. officials also say there are growing disagreements inside the Iranian regime. One camp, led by President Masoud Pezeshkian, is extremely worried about an economic collapse and believes Iran needs to reach a deal with the U.S. Another led by the commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, Ahmad Vahidi, rejects any concessions.

State of play: On Saturday, the head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, laid out new terms for reopening the strait — on top of those negotiated in the Oman agreement.

Zolghadr said in a statement that in order for the strait to reopen, the U.S. must:

  • "[N]ever threaten nor insult Iran in any language."
  • "[P]ermanently end the war against Iran and Iran's allies in Lebanon, Gaza, Yemen, and Iraq."
  • Lift the naval blockade and withdraw military forces from the surroundings of Iran.

He added a demand for full compensation for war damages, lifting all sanctions and the release of all Iranian frozen funds.

  • Until several weeks ago, these demands were a prerequisite for a nuclear deal. Now, Iran is presenting them as conditions just for reopening the strait.
  • A diplomat from one of the mediating countries said Zolghadr's statement reflected the political infighting within the regime.

Behind the scenes: U.S. officials said Trump was leaning toward resuming major combat operations against Iran a week ago but was convinced to de-escalate for now.

  • One of the officials said the fighting allowed the Iranian regime to avoid dealing with the consequences of the war, the damage to infrastructure and the deep economic crisis that has been created.
  • When Iran isn't engaged in war, it is forced to confront a grim reality with no real solutions at hand, the U.S. official said.
  • At the same time, the U.S. official said, around 8 million barrels of oil are going out of the Gulf every night through the southern lane of the Strait of Hormuz in coordination with the U.S. military. The U.S. is going to try and get more oil out as long as there is no deal.

What to watch: "This thing is not over. It's obviously not at the beginning. We're in the middle of the game, and we're applying a whole host of tools — diplomatic, economic, military tools — to ensure that we get the best outcome for the American people," Vice President Vance told Fox News on Saturday.

item.title: AOC is keeping two very big options open for 2028
item.description:
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) left the door open Sunday to either running for president in 2028 or challenging fellow New Yorker and Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer.

Why it matters: Ocasio-Cortez is emerging as a leading potential heir to the movement built by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), and whichever path she chooses could reshape the future of Democratic politics.

Driving the news: ABC's Jonathan Karl asked Ocasio-Cortez on "This Week" whether she would run for president, after noting a recent New Hampshire poll showed her leading the prospective Democratic field.

  • "I'm focused on winning the midterms. I'm running for Congress right now," she responded, before adding, "I haven't ruled out the possibility, and I'm very humbled to the tremendous amount of support out there."
  • When Karl asked whether running for Senate against Schumer was also possible, Ocasio-Cortez said that "anything is possible at this juncture."

The big picture: Ocasio-Cortez cast Abdul El-Sayed's victory in Michigan and a broader wave of insurgent Democratic victories as signs the party is undergoing a generational "renewal."

  • "Millennials are not, you know, punk kids anymore. We're grown adults with mortgages and kids," she said.
  • "That generation is starting to be decisive at the polls," she added. "We're taking the reins."

Zoom in: Ocasio-Cortez also sounded markedly more pragmatic than the young challenger who shocked the Democratic establishment in 2018.

  • Explaining why she has stayed out of primaries against House colleagues this cycle, Ocasio-Cortez said "politics is also a workplace." Her endorsements have largely targeted open seats, plus unseating incumbents in New York's state legislature.
  • She also distanced herself from some of the left's most polarizing positions in 2020.
  • "Rhetoric in that time is not rhetoric that we would use today," she said as she approvingly cited New York City Council member Chi Ossé's viral "Woke 1 was crazyyyy" response to one of his own old posts.

The bottom line: Ocasio-Cortez says her focus remains on the midterms.

  • But Sunday's interview did little to tamp down the 2028 speculation.

item.title: GOP may be stuck with Rep. Max Miller in Ohio
item.description:
Rep. Max Miller appeared to let a crucial Saturday withdrawal cutoff pass in Ohio's 7th Congressional District, effectively closing Republicans' last practical window to replace the embattled incumbent on the November ballot.

Why it matters: A district that favors Republicans has suddenly become a potential Democratic pickup as the GOP fights to preserve its narrow House majority, and Ohio law gave party leaders no room to replace Miller without his cooperation.

The latest: Miller's campaign spokesperson Abigail Angelos told The New York Times on Saturday that the two-term Republican would stay in the race despite domestic-abuse allegations he denies.

  • Miller did not return Axios' Saturday evening request for comment. On Friday, he had announced he would loan his campaign $1 million.
  • Miller would have needed to formally withdraw from the race Saturday to provide enough time for a required two-day notice before a GOP committee meeting to certify a replacement by Monday at 4pm ET.
  • The Cuyahoga County Board of Elections website still showed Miller as an active candidate early Sunday.

Catch up quick: Miller faces allegations of domestic abuse from his ex-wife, Emily Moreno, the daughter of Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio). Miller denies the allegations and has sued his ex-wife for defamation.

  • Miller previously sued ex-girlfriend Stephanie Grisham, a former White House press secretary, after she also accused him of abuse. He denied her claims and dropped the suit under a 2023 settlement. She sued him last month for allegedly violating the terms of that settlement's nondisparagement terms.
  • The House Ethics Committee said Tuesday it was investigating whether Miller "may have engaged in domestic violence and abuse or illegal drug use." Miller had requested an investigation into himself, but the committee did not say his request triggered the review.

State of play: Miller already passed an Aug. 5 threshold that could have triggered a special-election process for replacing a congressional nominee.

  • Ohio Republicans' last chance to replace him required he drop out and allow a committee made up of party officials to select his replacement before Monday at 4pm ET.

What he's said: Last week, Miller announced he wouldn't drop out in a video that brought even greater attention to the allegations.

  • He also released a curated dump of documents, photos and recordings. The files repeatedly named his young daughter and disclosed his ex-wife's home address, and his attorney later apologized for failing to remove a sensitive image.
  • Sen. Moreno, his former father-in-law, has called on Miller to leave Congress, saying Miller endangers his daughter and granddaughter and isn't fit to serve.

Between the lines: Miller faces Democrat Brian Poindexter, a union ironworker, in November.

  • President Trump carried the district by about 11 points in 2024, 10 points in 2020 and 12 points in 2016.

What to watch: The formal Monday certification deadline remains on the calendar, but unless Miller filed a timely withdrawal and the required committee notice was given, Republicans have no apparent way to certify a replacement based on his withdrawal.

item.title: Senate passes stopgap to avert pre-election shutdown
item.description:
The Senate passed a stopgap spending bill early Saturday that would keep the government funded through Dec. 11, moving Washington closer to avoiding another shutdown before the November midterms.

Why it matters: The bipartisan 90-6 vote would push the next government funding deadline past Election Day while offering some checks on the Trump administration.

State of play: The measure, which now goes to the House, generally maintains funding levels after the fiscal year ends Sept. 30, with a few negotiated exceptions.

  • It blocks the administration from implementing a proposed rule to give senior political appointees a larger role in reviewing federal grants, the Associated Press reported.
  • It prevents the administration from transferring money from other programs to the Border Patrol.
  • It rejects a White House request for $1 billion to begin work on President Trump's proposed new class of battleships.
  • And it delays for one month a looming ban on intoxicating hemp products, an issue that divided Senate Republicans.

Zoom in: The grants provision could prove one of the more consequential pieces of the short-term bill.

  • The Office of Management and Budget proposed rewriting rules in May to require senior political appointees review and consider whether discretionary grants advance the president's agenda.

The big picture: The Senate worked through the night, taking votes on the stopgap funding measure, the confirmation of Attorney General Todd Blanche and a failed voter ID measure, which would change voting requirements.

  • The vote reflects how eager lawmakers in both parties are to avoid putting another shutdown at the center of an election campaign.

What's next: The House will have to approve the Senate's changes after lawmakers return from their August recess.

  • If it does, Washington will have traded a possible pre-election shutdown fight for a potentially much larger post-election showdown in December over spending levels, Trump's grantmaking powers and the rest of the unfinished fiscal 2027 appropriations process.

item.title: Simplify: How to exponentially improve work, life
item.description:
Nothing has improved my work and life more than my new operating philosophy: Simplify.

  • I've seen such a dramatic improvement at Axios, and in my personal life, that I co-wrote a new book explaining step by step how it works. It's called "Simplify: Do 50% More with 50% Less."

Why it matters: Axios co-founders Jim VandeHei, Roy Schwartz and I dig deep into real-world experience and science to show you why most people waste years of their lives doing needless stuff out of habit or inertia.

  • You'll learn the three-step Simplify operating system we've personally stress-tested: Confront what you do, Delete what you shouldn't do, and Amplify what brings you joy and achievement.

💡 Simplify is a method and a mindset — a set of power tools to help you kill complexity in your life and work so you can be happier and more productive.

  • Smart Brevity, our first book, was about simplifying how you communicate. Simplify extends that superpower to how you lead, manage, work and live.

Why this? Simplify is a modern survival guide written for this wild, high-velocity AI moment.

  • We'll show you how to "say no" ... to delete ... to skip.

Why now? AI turns out to be the greatest complexity-generation machine ever invented. It mass-produces drafts, dashboards and action items, adding to the noise and distraction that engulf us.

  • Stunning stat: Research shows we spend two hours cleaning up each incident of AI workslop.

Why me? I'm excited for you to come along on my Simplify journey.

  • You'll learn what AT&T CEO John Stankey, who has spent years taming complexity at one of the world's oldest and most tradition-bound corporate giants, meant when he told me: "Stop till they squawk."
  • And a top executive told me how Meta became a "funner, faster" company.

The bottom line: Less is more. Simplify will give you more time for what matters.

  • Preorder here.
